prime.problem: "Which is best?" has no answer without n, the workload and the binding limit. Pick the fastest and you spend 512 MiB to hold 1,000 addresses; pick by worst case alone and you choose quicksort for nearly sorted data.
prime.fits: Second framing card. Requirements gave you the numbers; this card shows how to use them to choose, by pricing both sides and finding the break-even point. Simplicity, robustness and every estimation card reuse the habit.
expect: bitmap vs set vs sorted array
prime.goal: Price two options for a given n, find where they cross, and state the assumptions that make the answer hold.

attend: Why is the bitmap's size fixed at 512 MiB whatever you store, while the set's grows with n?
Where do the break-even points 8.3 million and 134 million addresses come from?
In rod cutting, what does the table r[0..n] remember that plain recursion recomputes, and what does that buy?
In the secretary problem, what do you give up by skipping the first k candidates?
When does the card say there is no trade-off at all?

must: A bitmap spends one bit on every possible key → size fixed by the universe (2³² bits = 512 MiB), not by n; a set spends ~64.6 B per stored key → the set wins below 536,870,912 / 64.6 ≈ 8.3 M keys, the bitmap above
Store each solved subproblem (r[j]) → no subproblem is solved twice → n + 1 cells of memory turn 2ⁿ recursive calls into O(n²) steps (55 steps for n = 10)
Skip k candidates to set a bar → the first better one is hired → too few skipped stops too early, too many risks skipping the best → k ≈ n/e hires the best ≈ 37% of the time
Input shape picks the algorithm → nearly sorted input is insertion sort's best case and last-pivot quicksort's worst → judging by worst-case Big-O alone picks wrong (2,009 vs 1,987,616 compares)
elevated: A Python set of ints costs a hash-table slot (33.5 B) plus an int object (31.0 B) per address → 16× the packed array → object overhead, not the data, sets the break-even
reference: the 32- vs 64-bit pointer figures (8,056 bytes for [None]*1000)

compress.prompt: In 3–5 sentences, explain "everything is a trade-off" using the IPv4 example: what each representation pays, and how you find the point where the answer flips. Then write one line each for rod cutting and the 37% rule saying what is traded for what.
checklist: each option buys one resource by paying another
the bitmap is O(1) and fixed-size; the set is O(1) and grows with n; the sorted array is small but O(log n) and slow to insert
the answer is a break-even n (8.3 M, 134 M)
the 37% rule trades interview count for a chance of the best, under strict assumptions

retrieve.q: Explain why "always pick the fastest" and "always pick the smallest" both fail for storing IPv4 addresses.
answer: fastest (bitmap) costs 512 MiB even for 1,000 addresses that fit in 4 kB as an array
smallest (sorted array) makes each insert shift up to n items, and above 134 M the bitmap is smaller anyway
the right choice depends on n and the operation mix

retrieve.q: Fill the rod-cutting table for j = 4 and j = 5 with prices 1, 5, 8, 9, 10: which first piece wins, and what does each row read?
answer: each row reads only earlier rows r[j − i]

retrieve.q: Your hiring manager can call back rejected candidates. Should you still use the 37% rule? Say which assumption fails and what that changes.
answer: the rule assumes no second chances, random order, only relative ranks, and only the single best counts
callbacks break "no second chances", so skipping costs less and a different strategy wins
the numbers are only as good as their assumptions

compare.q: Rod cutting here and the recursion-to-DP card both store subproblem answers. What is this card using DP to illustrate that the cs-3 card isn't, and what fails if the subproblems don't repeat?
answer: here DP is an example of trading memory for time
cs-3 teaches how to find the recursion and fill the table
if subproblems never repeat, the table stores answers nobody reuses: memory spent for nothing

compare.q: Insertion sort's worst case is O(n²), yet this card picks it for nearly sorted data. Which mechanism makes its cost depend on the input, and when does that stop helping?
answer: each swap fixes one out-of-order pair, so the work is the number of inversions
nearly sorted input has few inversions: 2,009 compares for 2,000 items
random or reversed input has ~n²/4 inversions, and it loses badly

predict.q: You only need to track which of 2²⁴ (16.7 million) user ids are active. Before computing: at roughly how many active ids does the bitmap stop being bigger than a Python set? Is it above or below the IPv4 break-even of 8.3 million?
predict.answer: Far below. The bitmap is now 2²⁴ / 8 = 2,097,152 B (2 MiB), so the set (≈ 64.6 B per id) is smaller only below 2,097,152 / 64.6 ≈ 32,000 ids. The break-even scales with the universe size: a smaller universe makes the fixed-size structure win much sooner.

apply.task: Change one price and redo the DP by hand: with the card's prices but p[4] = 11 instead of 9, recompute r[4] through r[10]. Then run rod_cut to check, and say which rows changed and why only those.
apply.done: Your table gives r = [0, 1, 5, 8, 11, 13, 17, 19, 22, 25, 30]: r[4] becomes 11 (sell whole) and r[7] becomes 19 (4 + 3 → 11 + 8); every other row is unchanged because its best plan never used a piece of length 4.
apply.hint: For each j, try every first piece i and read r[j − i] from rows you already filled.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: where the smaller universe puts the break-even?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the bitmap's size doesn't depend on n?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: stored subproblems → fewer calls, or fewer calls → O(n²)?
Could you name the assumptions behind the 37% rule without looking?
Where in your own work did you pick an option without pricing the other side?
